name: Latin
blurb: The language of Cicero, Virgil and Caesar, and the parent of the Romance languages.
facts: Romans wrote without spaces or lowercase letters. Both came centuries later.
Latin never died outright. It slowly turned into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian.
Over half of English vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it by way of French.
Classical Latin had no J, U or W. Iūlius was carved as IVLIVS.
The Vatican still issues documents in Latin, and its bank's ATMs offer Latin instructions.

units.title: Salvē
units.about: Greet people and name who they are

guide.p: Latin has no word for 'the' or 'a'. Context decides.
Latin likes to end a sentence with its verb.
A line over a vowel (ā) marks it as long. Romans rarely wrote it, but it changes pronunciation and sometimes meaning. You can type without them.

items.note: Said to one person. To a group: salvēte.

units.title: Familia
units.about: Family, home and who loves whom

guide.p: The subject and object are marked by endings, not word order. māter becomes mātrem as an object; fīlius becomes fīlium.
magna and parva are the feminine forms, used with feminine nouns like familia and domus. With masculine nouns they become magnus and parvus.
After in meaning 'in', the noun changes ending: domus becomes domō.

items.note: Originally the whole household, slaves included.

units.title: Cibus
units.about: Food, drink and the object ending

guide.p: aqua becomes aquam, cibus becomes cibum, pānis becomes pānem. Neuter nouns such as vīnum and lac look the same either way.
edit is 'he eats' or 'she eats'. Latin rarely needs a separate pronoun.
The present covers both English forms: edit is 'eats' and 'is eating'.

items.note: Careful: malum, with a short a, means 'evil'.

alt: the daughter is eating an apple

units.title: Rōma
units.about: The city, its roads and its gods

guide.p: Some nouns change shape a lot. rēx becomes rēgem as an object, urbs becomes urbem.
City names take no preposition for 'to'. Other places need ad.
Senātus Populusque Rōmānus, 'the Senate and People of Rome'. -que means 'and', tacked onto the end of a word.

units.title: Ego et tū
units.about: Talk about yourself and the person you meet

guide.p: -ō means 'I' and -s means 'you'. ego and tū are added only for emphasis.
sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he, she or it is'.
As objects, ego becomes mē and tū becomes tē.
mihi nōmen est … is literally 'to me the name is …'.
-ī marks 'I did'. Caesar reported a five-day war in 47 BC with three of them.
ex: I came, I saw, I conquered

guide.p: carpe is an order: 'seize!'. The line is from Horace, Odes 1.11.

omnia vincit Amor is Virgil (Eclogues 10). ālea iacta est is Caesar at the Rubicon, as told by Suetonius. cōgitō, ergō sum is Descartes, 1644, and et tū, Brūte is Shakespeare. Latin outlived Rome by a long way.

sentences.en: I came, I saw, I conquered

units.title: Herī
units.about: Tell what happened with the perfect tense

guide.p: The perfect tells what happened and is over. You met -ī in vēnī, vīdī, vīcī. The full set of endings is -ī, -istī, -it, -imus, -istis, -ērunt.
Many verbs change shape in the perfect, so learn the two together. Verbs like amō just add -v-.
One Latin form covers both English past tenses: fēcit is 'he made' or 'he has made'.
ex: what did you do? what have you done?

guide.p: Romans told stories as a chain of perfects, one event after another. herī 'yesterday' and tandem 'at last' set the scene.

units.title: Bellum
units.about: Soldiers, war and the third declension

guide.p: These nouns show their real stem only outside the subject form, so learn the object with the word, as with rēx, rēgem and urbs, urbem.
Third-declension plurals end in -ēs, as subject and as object. A plural subject takes a verb in -nt, and est becomes sunt.
ex: the general and the soldiers came

guide.p: puella and amīcus have plurals of their own: puellae, object puellās; amīcī, object amīcōs. The full present runs amō, amās, amat, amāmus, amātis, amant.
Neuter nouns look the same as subject and object, and their plural ends in -a: bellum, bella; corpus, corpora. arma 'weapons' and castra 'camp' exist only as plurals.
ex: I sing of arms and the man

guide.p: arma virumque canō opens the Aeneid, Rome's national epic. The man is Aeneas, the Trojan soldier the Romans claimed as their ancestor.

units.title: Maximus
units.about: Describe anything, and say what is bigger and best

guide.p: Adjectives match their noun's gender: bonus with masculine nouns, bona with feminine, bonum with neuter. The plurals are bonī, bonae, bona.
fortis 'brave' has one form for masculine and feminine, and forte for neuter. The plural is fortēs. An adjective can stand alone as a noun: fortēs is 'the brave'.
Add -ior for 'more' and -issimus for 'most' or 'very'. 'Than' is quam.
ex: the soldier is braver than the general

guide.p: The commonest adjectives change stem, like good, better, best. The neuters of maior and melior are maius and melius.
Third-declension nouns end in -e after in, just as templum became templō.
ex: a healthy mind in a healthy body

guide.p: mēns sāna in corpore sānō is Juvenal, Satires 10.356. fortissimī sunt Belgae is Caesar, Gallic War 1.1. fortēs fortūna iuvat is what Pliny the Elder said as he sailed toward Vesuvius, in his nephew's Letters 6.16.

units.title: Fābulae
units.about: Gods, myths and the words for who and which

guide.p: Roman gods matched Greek ones: Iuppiter is Zeus, Neptūnus is Poseidon, Venus is Aphrodite, Mārs is Ares and Minerva is Athena. Several have irregular object forms.
quī (masculine), quae (feminine) and quod (neuter) join a clause to a noun, taking the noun's gender.
ex: the god who rules the sea
the goddess who is in the temple

guide.p: When the relative is the object in its own clause it changes like a noun: quem, quam, quod. So quam can mean 'whom' as well as 'than'.
poēta looks like puella but is masculine, and so are its adjectives.
Iuppiter Optimus Maximus was Jupiter's official title, and his great temple on the Capitol was the heart of Roman religion.

items.note: Masculine, though it looks like puella.

guide.p: in, ex and ab take the ablative, the ending you met in in domō. It ends in -ā, -ō or -e. Before a consonant ex and ab often shrink to ē and ā.
With the object ending, in means 'into'. City names need no preposition at all: Rōmam 'to Rome', Rōmā 'from Rome'.
-ba- marks what was going on or used to happen. The endings are -bam, -bās, -bat, -bāmus, -bātis, -bant.
sum has its own imperfect: eram, erās, erat, erāmus, erātis, erant.
The imperfect paints the background, the perfect says what happened next.
ex: in urbe erāmus, et nūntius vēnit
we were in the city, and a messenger came

units.title: Crās
units.about: The future, infinitives and longer sentences

guide.p: Verbs like amō and videō add -b-: amābō, amābis, amābit, amābimus, amābitis, amābunt. Most others switch to -am, -ēs, -et, -ēmus, -ētis, -ent.
The future of sum is erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt.
ex: tomorrow we will be at the villa

guide.p: The infinitive ends in -re: amāre 'to love', vidēre 'to see', vincere 'to win', venīre 'to come'. 'To be' is esse.
possum 'I can' and volō 'I want' take an infinitive, usually just before them.
sed 'but' and quod 'because' join two clauses, each with its own verb.
ex: Rōmam vēnī, sed rēgem nōn vīdī
I came to Rome, but I did not see the king

guide.p: vīvere est cōgitāre is Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.111. vincere scīs, Hannibal is the cavalry commander Maharbal after Cannae in 216 BC, in Livy 22.51: you know how to win a battle, Hannibal, but not how to use the victory.

items.note: A different verb from volō 'I fly'.
